title: Distributed IDs & Time: Quick Revision
summary: Revision notes on generating unique, sortable IDs (auto-increment, UUID v4/v7, Snowflake, ticket servers) and on ordering events without a shared clock (NTP skew, Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks). Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: IDs and Clocks: The Mental Model
points: A distributed ID must be unique; the extras that matter are k-sortable (roughly time-ordered), compact, and generatable without coordination
Physical clocks answer 'when did it happen'; logical clocks answer 'what happened before what' and never need synchronized hardware
Happens-before (a → b): same process earlier, or send precedes receive; events with no such path are concurrent
Time-ordered keys keep B-tree inserts on the right edge (fast, cache-friendly); random keys cause page splits and cache misses

chapters.title: ID Schemes: Auto-increment, UUIDs, Snowflake, Ticket Servers
points: Auto-increment: 8-byte, sorted, tiny index, but a single writer is a bottleneck, it leaks row counts, and multi-master needs offset/step (node 1 gives 1,3,5; node 2 gives 2,4,6)
UUID v4: 122 random bits, 16 bytes, zero coordination, collision odds negligible, but unsorted so it fragments clustered indexes
UUID v7: 48-bit Unix-ms timestamp prefix plus random bits, so it is sortable like auto-increment and coordination-free like v4
Snowflake 64-bit layout: 1 sign bit, 41 bits ms timestamp (about 69 years from a custom epoch), 10 bits worker ID, 12 bits sequence (4096 IDs per ms per worker)
Ticket server (Flickr): a dedicated DB hands out ID blocks via REPLACE INTO; run two with odd/even steps, and clients cache a block to avoid a round trip per ID

chapters.title: Clock Skew, NTP and Why Wall Clocks Lie
points: Clock skew is the offset between two nodes' clocks; drift is the rate at which a clock gains or loses time (quartz is roughly tens of ppm)
NTP syncs to about ms on a LAN and tens of ms over the internet; it can step the clock backward, so time is not monotonic
Use a monotonic clock (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, System.nanoTime) for durations and timeouts, wall clock only for timestamps
Last-write-wins on wall clocks silently drops writes when the clock is skewed; the node with the fast clock always wins
Snowflake and UUIDv7 generators break on a backward clock jump: refuse to issue IDs, wait it out, or keep last_timestamp and bump the sequence

chapters.title: Logical Clocks: Lamport, Vector, Hybrid
points: Lamport clock: increment the counter on every local event; on send attach it; on receive set counter = max(local, received) + 1
Lamport guarantee: a → b implies L(a) < L(b); the converse is false, so equal or ordered timestamps cannot prove causality or concurrency
Vector clock: one counter per node; compare element-wise, and if neither vector dominates the other the events are concurrent (a conflict to resolve)
Vector clock cost grows with the number of nodes; Dynamo-style stores use it to keep sibling versions, then merge them or let the client resolve
Hybrid logical clock (HLC) = (physical time l, logical counter c), kept close to wall time yet causal; used by CockroachDB and MongoDB, with a bounded max-offset check

chapters.title: Ordering Guarantees in Partitioned Systems
points: Kafka orders only within a partition; pick the partition key (for example user_id) so related events share a partition
Total order across partitions needs a single partition, a sequencer, or consensus (Raft/Paxos), and costs throughput and latency
Per-key ordering plus idempotent consumers is the common design; consumers dedupe on event ID or sequence number
Retries with multiple in-flight requests can reorder messages; enable idempotent producers or limit in-flight requests per connection
Google Spanner TrueTime gives a bounded uncertainty interval [earliest, latest] and commit-wait for external consistency

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Choosing IDs and Clocks
points: Single DB, internal-only IDs: auto-increment (or bigint identity)
Public or distributed, no sorting needed: UUID v4; DB primary key at scale: UUID v7 or Snowflake
Need 64-bit compact sortable IDs: Snowflake, with worker ID assignment via ZooKeeper, etcd or config
Causal order only: Lamport; detect concurrency: vector clock; wall-time-like causal timestamps: HLC
Durations: monotonic clock; cross-node ordering: never raw wall-clock comparison
Sorting by ID only gives approximate time order across workers (ms-level skew)
Never expose sequential IDs as public identifiers without authorization checks (enumeration risk)
